answer.label: Not Winston Churchill — earliest full version is a 1938 Budweiser ad
answer.authorDates: Budweiser newspaper advertisement, 21 September 1938 · earliest known full wording
answer.sourceLine: Winston Churchill never said or wrote this. Quote Investigator ↗ traces the first complete version to a Budweiser advertisement in the Trenton Evening Times of 21 September 1938 — “success was never final and failure never fatal. It was courage that counted” — built from earlier partial sayings; the Churchill label was attached only in the 1960s.
answer.confidenceText: No Churchill source exists. The wording is traceable to 1930s American ad copy, not to Churchill’s speeches, books or letters.

trail: 1921 — George Matthew Adams’ syndicated essay “Finality” runs the line “Your success is not final—nor is your failure. You may always begin again,” per Quote Investigator’s citation trail ↗.

1938 — the first complete success/failure/courage version appears in a Budweiser newspaper advertisement; Quote Investigator suggests an ad copywriter synthesised it from the earlier partial sayings, see the full investigation ↗.
1968 — a Pennsylvania newspaper report of a Joe Paterno banquet speech carries the earliest located Churchill ascription, documented here ↗.
Today — the International Churchill Society still lists it among quotes “found nowhere in his canon,” on its falsely-attributed page ↗.
source.excerptNote: The 1938 advertising wording — past tense, and noticeably rougher than the polished modern sentence people attribute to Churchill.

author.name: George Matthew Adams
author.heading: About George Matthew Adams
author.bio: George Matthew Adams was an American columnist who founded the George Matthew Adams Newspaper Service, syndicating columns and comic strips to newspapers for five decades. His 1921 essay Finality carried the line “Your success is not final—nor is your failure. You may always begin again,” the earliest documented statement of the thought under a named author. He did not write the familiar modern sentence — that full wording surfaces later, in anonymous 1930s advertising copy.

misattribution.heading: The attribution trail
misattribution.intro: Churchill is one of the internet’s biggest magnets for unsourced uplift. This line is a textbook case: assembled from anonymous ad copy, then handed to the most quotable statesman available.

items.why: The International Churchill Society states plainly that this and similar lines are “broadly attributed to Winston Churchill… found nowhere in his canon,” and the reference collection Churchill by Himself files it under “Red Herrings: False Attributions” — see the Society’s falsely-attributed list ↗.

Quote Investigator’s earliest located Churchill ascription is a report in the Altoona Mirror of 1 April 1968, in which the Penn State coach quoted “Success is never final; failure is never fatal; the only thing that counts is courage” as Churchill’s — see the citation trail ↗.
Forbes magazine of 1 November 1948 printed “Success is never final and Failure never fatal. It’s courage that counts” credited to George F. Tilton, per Quote Investigator ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: The oldest full version yet found belongs to no famous person at all: a Budweiser advertisement in the Trenton Evening Times, 21 September 1938 — “success was never final and failure never fatal. It was courage that counted” — as documented by Quote Investigator ↗.

context.heading: How a beer ad became a Churchill quote
lead: The sentence has an odd pedigree: the pieces existed before anyone assembled them. A 1921 syndicated essay called Finality, by columnist George Matthew Adams, told readers “Your success is not final—nor is your failure. You may always begin again.” The bolt-together version — success, failure and courage in one breath — shows up in a 1938 Budweiser newspaper advertisement ↗.

Churchill enters the story a generation later. By 1968 the Penn State coach Joe Paterno was quoting it to high-school athletes as Churchill’s, and the newspaper report repeated the credit. From there it hardened into internet fact — recited in commencement speeches, printed on posters, and used by Ron DeSantis when he ended his 2024 presidential campaign, which prompted a fresh round of fact-checks ↗.
context.pull: A slogan written to sell beer, wearing a statesman’s voice.
